cases.abstract: Strong performance from vision Transformers need not imply that self-attention is the decisive ingredient for visual recognition. We investigate this distinction by progressively redesigning ResNet into ConvNeXt, a convolutional backbone that adopts hierarchical Transformer design choices without attention. The study first strengthens the training recipe, then examines computation across stages, spatial and channel mixing, and block-level normalization and activation. Depthwise spatial convolutions and expanded pointwise layers retain the separation of operations found in Transformer blocks, while normalized stage transitions stabilize the final architecture. At 384 x 384 resolution, ConvNeXt-B trained on ImageNet-1K achieves 85.1% top-1 accuracy, compared with 84.5% for Swin-B, and processes 95.7 rather than 85.1 images per second on a V100 GPU. ImageNet-22K pretraining followed by ImageNet-1K fine-tuning yields 87.8% for ConvNeXt-XL. Evaluations with standard detection and segmentation heads also show competitive performance on COCO and ADE20K. Together, these results support modernized convolution as an alternative to Swin for the tested recognition workloads and show that several useful Transformer design choices do not depend on attention.
cases.methods: A ConvNeXt block first applies a 7 x 7 depthwise convolution, which mixes spatial information independently within each channel. Layer normalization is followed by two 1 x 1 convolutions that expand channel width fourfold and then restore it, with a single GELU between them and a residual connection around the block. Placing the spatial operation before expansion keeps its channel count low, making a larger receptive field affordable while leaving channel mixing to dense pointwise layers. The surrounding network uses a nonoverlapping 4 x 4 stem and separate, normalized downsampling between stages. To evaluate the redesign, successive architectures share a 300-epoch AdamW training recipe on ImageNet-1K, with roughly comparable FLOPs; small-regime accuracies average three seeds. This design links the final backbone to a sequence of measured changes rather than treating attention removal alone as the explanation for performance.
cases.results: The modernization results show that training and architecture both contribute, but individual substitutions are not uniformly beneficial. Updating the ResNet-50 training recipe raises top-1 accuracy from 76.1% to 78.8%, so comparison with the original baseline would over-credit architectural changes. Under the fixed recipe, replacing ReLU with GELU leaves accuracy at 80.6%, whereas retaining only one activation raises it to 81.3%. Separate downsampling initially causes training to diverge; adding normalization at resolution transitions and after pooling stabilizes the model and brings the final sequence to 82.0%, versus Swin-T's 81.3%. These are successive configurations, so each gain is conditional on earlier changes. Transfer results extend the comparison beyond classification: with ImageNet-22K pretraining and Cascade Mask R-CNN under a 3x schedule, ConvNeXt-B reaches 54.0 box AP and 46.9 mask AP on COCO, compared with 53.0 and 45.8 for Swin-B. The combined evidence favors the redesigned backbone in these settings, not an unconditional benefit from every Transformer-inspired choice.
cases.notes: The roadmap reports 82.0% for the final small configuration, whereas the main classification table reports 82.1% for ConvNeXt-T; the results paragraph uses the roadmap value and does not combine these records. Stepwise ablations are conditional on previously adopted changes, not a factorial attribution of independent effects. ImageNet-1K-only training and ImageNet-22K pretraining are kept separate. EfficientNetV2-L retains the highest listed ImageNet-1K-only accuracy, so the abstract's advantage is scoped to Swin-B. No statistical significance is inferred from seed means.

cases.abstract: Fast radiance-field methods reduce training cost, but their renderers and reconstruction quality can still limit interactive exploration of captured scenes. We represent a static scene as an optimized set of anisotropic 3D Gaussians, initialized from sparse structure-from-motion points and carrying opacity and spherical-harmonic appearance. This explicit representation supports differentiable image formation without estimating surface normals. Adaptive cloning and splitting allocate primitives where reconstruction remains inadequate, while a tile-based rasterizer sorts splats and blends them with a backward pass that imposes no fixed limit on contributing primitives. On held-out views from three real-scene datasets, the 30,000-iteration configuration renders at dataset-average rates of 134-154 frames per second on an A6000 GPU after roughly 27-42 minutes of training. It exceeds Mip-NeRF360 in SSIM on all three datasets, although PSNR is lower on the Mip-NeRF360 dataset. The rendering speed therefore accompanies competitive, rather than uniformly superior, reconstruction quality. This tradeoff requires hundreds of megabytes of stored parameters and leaves artifacts in weakly observed regions; approximate visibility handling can also produce popping during viewpoint changes.
cases.methods: Rendering projects each Gaussian's covariance into image space and assigns its footprint to 16 x 16 pixel tiles. Gaussian instances receive keys combining tile identity and view-space depth, enabling one GPU radix sort to prepare all tile lists. Threads then blend colors and opacity front to back, stopping at opacity saturation. Avoiding per-pixel sorting makes anisotropic splatting efficient, but the shared depth order is an approximation. For differentiation, the renderer traverses those lists backward and reconstructs intermediate opacity factors from saved accumulations, rather than storing a variable-length history for every pixel. No fixed primitive-count cutoff is imposed on gradients. The image loss combines L1 error with D-SSIM and updates Gaussian geometry, opacity, and appearance. Interleaved density control clones small Gaussians or splits large ones when positional gradients indicate unresolved reconstruction, so the sparse initialization can gain detail as optimization proceeds.
cases.results: On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, training for 30,000 rather than 7,000 iterations raises PSNR from 25.60 to 27.21 dB and reduces LPIPS from 0.279 to 0.214, while rendering falls from 160 to 134 frames per second and stored parameters grow from 523 to 734 MB. Additional optimization thus improves reconstruction at a measurable cost in model size and rendering speed. Relative to Mip-NeRF360, the longer-trained model has higher SSIM and lower LPIPS but lower PSNR, making the quality comparison metric-dependent. Its roughly 42-minute training on an A6000 cannot be read as a matched-GPU speedup over Mip-NeRF360's 48 GPU-hours, obtained from four A100 GPUs running for 12 hours. The three-scene ablation explains why rendering shortcuts must preserve useful gradients: limiting updates to ten frontmost Gaussians lowers average 30,000-iteration PSNR from 26.05 to 19.19 dB across Truck, Garden, and Bicycle. Poorly covered regions and occasional popping remain unresolved, despite the speed of the full renderer.
cases.notes: Main real-scene metrics use every eighth photograph as a held-out test view; Mip-NeRF360 metrics on its own dataset are adopted from its paper. Other dataset comparisons use reruns. Training time for that baseline is a single-GPU-equivalent compute total, not 48 hours of measured wall time on the A6000. Ablation inputs were manually downsampled from high-resolution images and should not be treated as the main evaluation's identical input pipeline. Random-initialization success on synthetic bounded scenes is not generalized to real captures, where background reconstruction degrades. Memory figures in the quantitative table cover stored optimized parameters, not training peaks or rasterizer workspace.
